summary_profile.description: Malaria is a potentially life-threatening parasitic disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted to humans exclusively through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. It is most common in tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, with Plasmodium falciparum being the deadliest species responsible for the majority of severe cases and deaths. Without prompt diagnosis and correct treatment, uncomplicated malaria can rapidly progress to severe, multi-organ disease resulting in coma or death — particularly in children under 5, pregnant women, and non-immune travellers.
common_symptoms: Fever — often high-grade; may be cyclical (every 48 or 72 hours depending on species)
Chills and shaking rigors — classic paroxysm begins with intense chills
Sweating — follows the fever phase; soaks clothing and bedding
Flu-like illness (early symptoms are often mistaken for influenza or common cold)
severe_symptoms: Altered consciousness, confusion, or unresponsiveness (cerebral malaria)
Seizures or convulsions — two or more within 24 hours
Coma — unrousable coma is hallmark of cerebral malaria (mainly P. falciparum)
Respiratory distress — deep, laboured breathing due to metabolic acidosis
Difficulty breathing or pulmonary oedema (fluid in lungs)
Severe anaemia — extreme pallor, weakness, fatigue due to red blood cell destruction
Jaundice — yellowing of skin and whites of eyes due to haemolysis and liver involvement
Dark, red, or black urine (haemoglobinuria / blackwater fever) — indicates massive haemolysis and renal failure risk
Kidney failure — oliguria or anuria
Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) — especially in children and pregnant women; may cause unconsciousness
Circulatory shock (cold clammy skin, hypotension, rapid weak pulse)
Abnormal bleeding or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Extreme weakness or prostration — inability to sit or stand unsupported
Hyperparasitaemia — parasitised red blood cells greater than 5% of total
Spleen rupture — sudden severe left-side abdominal pain and haemorrhagic shock (mainly P. vivax)
High fever above 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to antipyretics
causes: Bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito injecting Plasmodium sporozoites into the bloodstream — primary and most common route
Plasmodium falciparum — most dangerous species; causes the majority of severe malaria cases and deaths; responsible for cerebral malaria
Plasmodium vivax — most widespread globally; causes relapsing malaria due to dormant liver stages (hypnozoites); major cause in South Asia and Latin America
Plasmodium ovale — similar to P. vivax; milder disease; capable of liver dormancy and relapse; mainly West Africa
Plasmodium malariae — causes mild, chronic quartan (72-hour cycle) infection; can persist for years untreated; associated with kidney disease
Plasmodium knowlesi — zoonotic species naturally infecting macaque monkeys in Southeast Asia; can cause rapidly progressive severe disease in humans
Parasites injected as sporozoites travel to liver, multiply, then invade and rupture red blood cells causing all clinical symptoms
Blood transfusion with infected donor blood — rare non-mosquito transmission
Organ transplantation from infected donor — rare
Congenital transmission — infected mother to newborn during pregnancy or delivery (vertical transmission)
Sharing contaminated needles or syringes — rare; reported in drug users
Malaria is NOT spread person-to-person like a cold or flu, and is NOT sexually transmitted
risk_factors: Living in or travelling to malaria-endemic tropical and subtropical regions — Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands
Children under 5 years of age — most vulnerable group; account for the majority of malaria deaths globally
Pregnant women — greatly increased susceptibility; higher risk of severe disease, miscarriage, stillbirth, and low birth weight
Non-immune travellers — people travelling from non-endemic to endemic countries with no prior immunity
Lack of mosquito bite prevention — not using insecticide-treated bed nets, repellents, or protective clothing
Outdoor exposure at night — Anopheles mosquitoes are most active from dusk to dawn
HIV/AIDS and immunosuppressive conditions — impaired immunity increases severity
Asplenia (absence or dysfunction of spleen) — spleen is critical for clearing parasitised red blood cells
Sickle cell disease (protective against P. falciparum but does not eliminate risk)
Lack of access to healthcare or preventive measures — a major driver of malaria burden in endemic regions
Partial immunity loss — residents of endemic areas who have moved away lose their acquired partial immunity
Poor sanitation and stagnant water near homes — creates Anopheles mosquito breeding sites
Failure to take or complete chemoprophylaxis before and during travel to endemic areas
Visiting friends and relatives (VFR travellers) — often underestimate their risk and skip prophylaxis
diagnosis_methods: Thick and thin blood smear microscopy (Giemsa-stained) — gold standard; identifies species, quantifies parasite density, and guides treatment; results must be available within 24 hours
Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) — detects malaria antigens (HRP2, pLDH, aldolase) in blood; fast results in under 20 minutes; used when microscopy is unavailable
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) — highest sensitivity; identifies species and detects low-level parasitaemia; used in reference labs and for confirmatory testing
Blood culture — not used for malaria; blood smear is required
Complete blood count (CBC) — reveals anaemia (low haemoglobin), thrombocytopenia (low platelets), and leucopenia
Liver function tests (LFTs) — elevated bilirubin and aminotransferases (AST, ALT) in malaria
Renal function tests — elevated creatinine and urea indicate acute kidney injury in severe cases
Blood glucose — mandatory; hypoglycaemia is a common life-threatening complication especially in children
Arterial blood gas — reveals metabolic acidosis in severe malaria
Chest X-ray — indicated if pulmonary oedema or pneumonia is clinically suspected
Clinical rule: Always confirm a clinical diagnosis of malaria with a laboratory test — empiric treatment without confirmation is NOT recommended
Important: Malaria must be considered in any febrile patient who has travelled to or returned from a malaria-endemic area within the past 12 months — even if prophylaxis was taken
treatment_options: Malaria is CURABLE with correct antimalarial medication — early diagnosis and prompt treatment are essential
Treatment regimen depends on: infecting Plasmodium species, clinical severity (uncomplicated vs severe), geographic drug-resistance patterns, patient age, pregnancy status, and prior antimalarial use
Uncomplicated malaria (non-falciparum, non-knowlesi) — treated with oral antimalarial drugs; patients can usually be managed as outpatients
Uncomplicated P. falciparum / P. knowlesi — requires urgent initiation of appropriate oral therapy; close monitoring essential
Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) — first-line WHO-recommended treatment for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria worldwide
Chloroquine — preferred treatment for P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae in regions where parasites remain sensitive; no longer effective for P. falciparum in most areas
Radical cure for P. vivax and P. ovale — requires primaquine or tafenoquine to eliminate dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) and prevent relapse; G6PD testing mandatory before use
Severe malaria (any species) — medical emergency; requires hospitalisation and parenteral (intravenous or intramuscular) antimalarial therapy
Intravenous artesunate — first-line treatment for severe malaria; has replaced quinine as preferred agent
Step-down therapy — after parenteral treatment, complete a full 3-day course of oral ACT once patient can tolerate oral medications
Supportive care for severe malaria — intensive monitoring, IV fluids, blood glucose management, blood transfusion for severe anaemia, seizure control, oxygen therapy
Pregnant women — treat as medical emergency; quinine plus clindamycin in first trimester; ACT acceptable in second and third trimesters for severe malaria
Chemoprophylaxis — travellers to endemic areas should take prescription antimalarial drugs before, during, and after travel
Standby emergency treatment (SBET) — prescribed for travellers in very remote areas where immediate medical care is not available
medications: Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used ACT; first-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria; oral 6-dose course over 3 days
Artesunate-amodiaquine — ACT; used in Africa and some parts of Asia
Artesunate-mefloquine — ACT; used in Southeast Asia
Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine — ACT; oral; used in Africa and Southeast Asia
Artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine — ACT; used in some African countries
Intravenous artesunate — first-line treatment for severe malaria; dose: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 hours then daily; preferred over quinine
Intramuscular artesunate or artemether — when IV access is not immediately available in severe malaria
Quinine sulfate — oral; alternative for uncomplicated drug-resistant P. falciparum; always combined with doxycycline, tetracycline, or clindamycin
Intravenous quinine — alternative for severe malaria when artesunate is unavailable; requires cardiac monitoring
Chloroquine phosphate — oral; treatment for chloroquine-sensitive P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae; no longer effective for P. falciparum in most regions
Hydroxychloroquine — alternative to chloroquine for sensitive species
Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) — oral; treatment for uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum; also used for chemoprophylaxis in travellers
Mefloquine (Lariam) — oral; alternative treatment and weekly chemoprophylaxis; avoid in psychiatric illness and seizure disorders
Primaquine — oral; radical cure for P. vivax and P. ovale to eliminate hypnozoites; G6PD testing mandatory before use; contraindicated in pregnancy and infants under 6 months
Tafenoquine — newer alternative to primaquine for radical cure; single-dose regimen; G6PD testing mandatory; contraindicated in pregnancy
Doxycycline — oral; used with quinine for drug-resistant P. falciparum; also used as chemoprophylaxis
Clindamycin — oral; used with quinine when doxycycline is contraindicated (pregnancy, children under 8 years)
Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (Fansidar) — used in intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) and seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC); limited treatment use due to resistance
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) — for symptomatic fever control; safe in all ages including pregnancy; does NOT treat malaria itself
lifestyle_home_remedies: Rest completely — malaria causes significant physical exhaustion; adequate rest supports recovery
Stay well hydrated — drink plenty of clean water and fluids to prevent dehydration, especially during febrile episodes
Take all prescribed antimalarial medications on schedule and complete the full course — even if feeling better; incomplete treatment causes relapse and drug resistance
Use insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) every night — even while ill, to prevent re-infection and transmission to mosquitoes and others
Keep windows and doors closed or screened, especially at night when Anopheles mosquitoes are active
Apply EPA-approved insect repellent containing DEET, icaridin, or picaridin to exposed skin at dusk and at night
Wear long-sleeved shirts, long trousers, and socks in the evenings to reduce mosquito biting
Monitor temperature regularly — seek immediate medical attention if fever returns or worsens after initial improvement
Avoid self-medicating with over-the-counter fever medicines alone without seeking diagnosis — fever in a malaria-endemic area or after recent travel requires urgent medical evaluation
Eliminate standing water near your home (old tyres, containers, pots) — prevents Anopheles mosquito breeding
Keep indoor environment cool and dry — mosquitoes prefer warm humid conditions
diet_recommended: Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) or clean water — essential for replacing fluids lost during high fever and sweating
Light, easily digestible carbohydrates — white rice, plain porridge, bread — for energy when appetite is reduced
Bananas and soft fruits — provide potassium and quick energy; easy to eat during illness
Warm broths and soups — maintain hydration and provide electrolytes and protein
Coconut water — natural electrolyte replacement during febrile illness
Leafy green vegetables and iron-rich foods (lentils, beans, spinach) — support recovery from malaria-associated anaemia
Protein-rich foods (eggs, lean meats, legumes) — support immune function and tissue repair
Vitamin C-rich foods (citrus fruits, guava, tomatoes) — enhance iron absorption from plant sources; important for anaemia recovery
Small frequent meals — preferred over large meals when nausea and loss of appetite are present
Glucose or sugar-containing fluids — important for preventing or correcting hypoglycaemia, especially in children
diet_to_avoid: Alcohol — impairs immune function, interferes with antimalarial medications, and worsens dehydration; strictly avoid during treatment
Raw or undercooked foods — at risk of secondary gastrointestinal infections that complicate recovery in an already compromised patient
Heavily spiced or fried foods — may worsen nausea and vomiting which are common malaria symptoms
Dairy products (in some patients) — may cause or worsen gastrointestinal discomfort during acute illness
Grapefruit juice — may interact with certain antimalarial medications including atovaquone-proguanil (do not take with fatty foods alone without protein)
Excessive caffeine — dehydrating; may worsen headache and sleep disruption
Large, heavy meals — difficult to digest and worsen nausea during acute febrile illness
Unpurified or untreated water — risk of additional waterborne infections in endemic areas
complications: Cerebral malaria — parasitised red blood cells block small blood vessels of the brain; causes seizures, coma, swelling, and brain damage; 15–20% case fatality rate even with treatment; mainly caused by P. falciparum
Severe anaemia — massive destruction of red blood cells reduces oxygen delivery to tissues; may require blood transfusion
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and pulmonary oedema — fluid accumulation in lungs causes severe breathing difficulty; mortality up to 80% in pregnancy
Acute kidney injury — renal failure due to microvascular obstruction and haemoglobin deposition; may require dialysis
Blackwater fever — massive haemolysis causing haemoglobinuria (dark urine); leads to acute kidney failure; associated with P. falciparum and quinine use
Hypoglycaemia — dangerously low blood sugar; especially common in children, pregnant women, and those treated with quinine (which stimulates insulin release); can cause unconsciousness and death
Metabolic acidosis — accumulation of lactic acid in blood; causes deep laboured breathing and cardiovascular collapse
Splenomegaly and splenic rupture — enlarged spleen can rupture causing life-threatening internal bleeding; more common with P. vivax
Circulatory shock and multi-organ failure — algid malaria; high mortality
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — abnormal clotting cascade leading to simultaneous bleeding and clotting
Relapse of P. vivax and P. ovale malaria — dormant liver hypnozoites reactivate weeks to years after initial infection if radical cure with primaquine/tafenoquine was not completed
Recrudescence — parasites survive at sub-detectable levels after inadequate treatment; resurgence of P. falciparum or P. malariae without liver stage
Pregnancy complications — miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight, maternal death; P. falciparum causes placental malaria
Congenital malaria — transmission from infected mother to newborn during delivery
Hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (HMS) — chronic immune-mediated massive splenomegaly from repeated malaria infections
Neurological sequelae in children — epilepsy, learning difficulties, behavioural and cognitive impairment after cerebral malaria
summary_profile.when_to_see_doctor: See a healthcare provider as soon as possible if you experience fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, or any flu-like symptoms AND you live in or have travelled to a malaria-endemic area within the past 12 months — even if you took antimalarial prophylaxis during your trip. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen. Malaria can deteriorate very rapidly, especially P. falciparum, which can become life-threatening within 24–48 hours of symptom onset. Always remind your doctor of your recent travel history. Early diagnosis and prompt correct treatment give the best chance of full recovery and prevent progression to severe, potentially fatal disease.
emergency_signs: Altered consciousness, confusion, drowsiness, or inability to be woken normally (cerebral malaria)
Seizures or convulsions — especially more than one in 24 hours
Severe difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or laboured deep breathing (respiratory distress)
Dark red, brown, or black urine (haemoglobinuria / blackwater fever) — indicates severe haemolysis and kidney failure
High fever greater than 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to paracetamol
Signs of severe anaemia — extreme pallor of skin, lips, and inside of eyelids
Inability to stand or sit unsupported (extreme prostration)
Signs of dehydration — no urination, dry mouth, sunken eyes
Persistent vomiting preventing oral medication intake
Abnormal bleeding — from gums, nose, or skin (petechiae, purpura) suggesting DIC
Signs of shock — cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, very low blood pressure
Jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) combined with fever after travel to endemic area
Hypoglycaemia signs — sweating, trembling, confusion, unconsciousness — especially in children and pregnant women
Any fever with malaria symptoms in a child under 5 years who lives in or recently visited a malaria-endemic area — this is a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation
